To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the timing of antiretro-viral therapy is critical and should be based on the immunological status of the patient.

the timing of antiretrovirals is crucial for the success of the therapy, that a CD4 cell count <200 cells/microl should trigger treatment, that a CD8 response is essential for viral control and that the immune system is the key player in viral eradication.

the initiation of treatment is best delayed until the CD4 T cell count falls below 500 cells/μl, and that the timing of the treatment is best determined by the clinical status and the CD4 T- cell count of the patient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of HIV infection and antiretrovial therapy on the host immune system.
the immunological aspects of the timing of treatment.

the timing of the initiation of effective antiviral therapy, the immunological consequences of the timing of therapy and the development of new strategies that will optimise long-term treatment success.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the initiation of antiretrovirals should not be delayed until a patient has developed an opportunistic illness, and that the initiation of effective antiviral therapy should be based on the patient's clinical condition, CD4 T-cell counts and viral load.

the optimal timing of antiretro-viral therapy should be individualised and based upon the patient's immune status, the viral load, and the ability to maintain and/or restore HIV-1-specific T-cell responses.

the initiation of antiretro-viral therapy is a complex process that should be based on an individual assessment of the patient's clinical and immunological status and that the timing of treatment is critical for the success of the therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the timing of initiation and duration of therapy are important considerations for the long-term success and survival of the patient.
the timing of antiretrovirals is crucial for the long-term outcome of therapy.
the time to begin antiretrovirus therapy is when CD4 T cells fall below 500 cells/µl, but that the time to start is also when the patient's quality of life is compromised.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to understand how the immune system works and how it is affected by HIV-1 and by the antiretrovirus therapies.
the time of initiation of effective ART has a profound effect on the success of the therapy and on the long-term prognosis of patients with HIV-1 infection.
the timing of initiation should be individualised, based on the patient's CD4 cell count, viral load, clinical condition, comorbidities and the patient's willingness to adhere to treatment.
